CausalChain: Increased ECM stiffness -> Activation of integrin‐β5 on Kupffer cells and monocytes -> Activation of FAK/MEK/ERK cascade and HIF1α stabilization -> Polarization of TAMs towards M2 phenotype -> Secretion of immunosuppressive cytokines and tumor progression -> Modulation of ECM stiffness and inhibition of integrin‐β5/FAK/MEK/ERK -> Repolarization of TAMs to M1 phenotype -> Enhanced cytotoxic T cell infiltration and anti-tumor responses
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that by combining the modulation of ECM stiffness through advanced, tunable biomaterials with the precise, nanoparticle-mediated inhibition of the integrin‐β5/FAK/MEK/ERK signaling pathway, it is possible to reprogram tumor-associated macrophages in HCC from an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype to an immunostimulatory M1 phenotype. This reprogramming, achieved via real-time mechanobiological feedback systems and targeted drug delivery platforms, will enhance cytotoxic T cell infiltration and synergize with existing immunotherapies to combat tumor progression. Specifically, the strategy involves (1) engineering ECM-mimetic scaffolds with adjustable stiffness parameters, (2) deploying integrin‐β5 inhibitor-conjugated nanoparticles to selectively disrupt the FAK/MEK/ERK-mediated stabilization of HIF1α, and (3) utilizing advanced imaging modalities coupled with computational modeling to ensure optimal targeting and dosing.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression is strongly influenced by the biophysical properties of its tumor microenvironment, particularly extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness. Recent evidence indicates that increased ECM stiffness activates integrin‐β5 on Kupffer cells and infiltrating monocytes, triggering the FAK/MEK/ERK cascade and stabilizing HIF1α, ultimately driving tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs) toward an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype. Here, we hypothesize that a dual intervention strategy employing advanced biomaterial-based modulation of ECM mechanics combined with targeted nanotherapeutics—such as integrin‐β5 inhibitor-conjugated nanoparticles—can disrupt the integrin‐β5/FAK/MEK/ERK signaling cascade. This intervention is expected to reprogram TAMs from the pro-tumorigenic M2 to the anti-tumorigenic M1 phenotype, thereby enhancing cytotoxic T cell infiltration and improving the efficacy of HCC immunotherapies. Furthermore, contemporary imaging and mechanobiological computational modeling can be leveraged to optimize the precise level of ECM stiffness modulation required for effective reprogramming, while real-time monitoring ensures targeted delivery and minimizes off-target effects.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that modifying ECM stiffness or disrupting the integrin‐β5/FAK/MEK/ERK pathway could repolarize TAMs from an M2 to an M1 phenotype to improve immunotherapy in HCC. Our revised hypothesis retains the original causal chain—(1) ECM stiffness increases integrin‐β5 activation, leading to FAK/MEK/ERK signaling and HIF1α stabilization, which (2) drives M2 polarization of TAMs and supports tumor progression; (3) conversely, dampening this signaling promotes M1 repolarization and anti-tumor immunity. However, we have enhanced its practical implementability by incorporating contemporary technological capabilities: advanced biomaterials for precise ECM stiffness modulation, targeted nanoparticle systems for selective pathway inhibition, and real-time imaging coupled with computational models for optimization of intervention parameters. These additions strengthen mechanistic clarity and translational potential while directly addressing the observed evidence and criticisms.
